beats.caption: A tiny oscillator sets the beat for the whole board
beats.text: Every digital chip needs a clock. On this board a small crystal oscillator makes a reference tone and a clock generator/buffer chip multiplies and copies it to the GPU, the controller and every high-speed link.

beats.caption: Inside: a slice of quartz between two electrodes
beats.text: Open the oscillator's ceramic package and there is a thin quartz blank held on conductive mounts, with metal electrodes on both faces, and a small driver chip. MEMS oscillators replace the quartz with a tiny silicon resonator, which is SiTime's approach.

beats.caption: It rings at one exact frequency
beats.text: Quartz is piezoelectric: a voltage bends it, and bending makes a voltage. The driver keeps it ringing at its natural frequency (here, as often, ~25-156 MHz), turning the vibration into a square-wave clock accurate to parts per million.

beats.caption: The clock fans out to every chip in step
beats.text: The clock generator multiplies the reference with phase-locked loops and buffers copies out on matched traces, so the GPU, controller and SerDes all tick in step. A switch or AI server carries dozens of these outputs.

beats.caption: Jitter: a few hundred femtoseconds can break a link
beats.text: Real edges wobble a little in time (jitter). At 112-224 Gb/s per lane a bit lasts only a few picoseconds, so SerDes need clocks with jitter in the tens of femtoseconds. Faster links mean more, better timing parts per box: SiTime (SITM), Renesas (RNECY), TI (TXN), Microchip (MCHP), Skyworks (SWKS).
